source_text: τῶν ἁγίων ἐμπίπλησι φρένα. Τοιγάρτοι καὶ ἱεροὶ καὶ εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας γένοιντο ἂν ἐξαίρετοι τῷ Θεῷ. Νεφροὶ δὲ δὴ πάλιν, εἰς τύπον ἂν εἶεν τῆς εἰς νοῦν ἔσω διακριτικῆς ἐνεργείας· καθ' ἣν ἀπόβλητον μὲν, τὸ πεφυκὸς ἀδικεῖν, αἱρετὸν δὲ καὶ ἀξιόληπτον ποιεῖται τὸ ὠφελοῦν. Γράφει δὲ καὶ ὁ θεσπέσιος Παῦλος· «Πάντα δοκιμάζοντες, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε, ἀπὸ παντὸς εἴδους πονηροῦ ἀπέχεσθε.» Οὐκοῦν ἐπειδήπερ διακριτικὸν ἐν σώματι μόριον ὁ νεφρὸς (ἀποκρίνει γὰρ εὖ μάλα τὰ περιττὰ, τὸ χρηστόν τε καὶ ὠφελοῦν ἐνιεὶς τῇ φύσει, καὶ διανέμων εὐτέχνως, οἷς ἂν καὶ ὅσον διανέμεσθαι πρέποι), μεταληπτέον εἰκότως εἰς νοῦ διάκρισιν τοὺς νεφρούς. Ἱεροὶ τοιγαροῦν καὶ ἀνάθημα Θεῷ, τῶν ἁγίων οἱ νεφροὶ, τουτέστιν, ἥνπερ ἂν ἔχοιεν ἐν νῷ διάκρισιν. Δόκιμοι γὰρ τραπεζῖται καὶ ἀκριβεῖς, οἱ Θεῷ προσκείμενοι, κατακιβδηλεύοντες μὲν τὸ φαῦλον ἀεὶ, ψήφῳ γε μὴν τῇ παγκάλῳ τιμᾷν εἰωθότες τὸ τελοῦν εἰς ὄνησιν. Ὧδε γὰρ οἶμαι καὶ τὸν θεσπέσιον Μελῳδὸν εὐδοκιμεῖν εἰωθότα διακεκραγέναι πρὸς τὸν Θεόν· «Ὅτι σὺ ἐκτήσω τοὺς νεφρούς μου, Κύριε.» Ὁ δέ γε λοβὸς τοῦ ἥπατος, οὐδὲν ἧττον ἡμῖν ὑποφαίνει, ἢ ψυχῆς ἐνέργειαν, ἤτοι φρενὸς κίνησιν, καθ' ἣν ἴεται πρὸς ἐπιθυμίας. Ἐξηκριβωκότες δὲ τὰ τοιάδε τινὲς, οὐδὲν ὀκνοῦντές φασιν, ὡς ἐν ἥπατι τὰς ἐπιθυμίας ἅπαν ἔχει ζῶον. Ἀναθετέον δὴ οὖν καὶ τὸν λοβὸν τοῦ ἥπατος τῷ Θεῷ, τουτέστιν, αὐτὴν οἱονείπως ἁπάσης ἐπιθυμίας ἡμῶν τὴν πηγὴν, κατά γε τὸν ψάλλοντα Μελῳδόν· «Κύριε, ἐναντίον σου πᾶσα ἡ ἐπιθυμία μου.» Σεμνύνεται δέ τις ἐφ' ἑαυτῷ, καὶ τὴν ὧδε σεπτὴν καὶ ἀξιάγαστον ἀναμέλπει φωνὴν, εἰ πρός γε δὴ μόνον τὸ τῷ Θεῷ δοκοῦν τὰς ὀρέξεις ἔχοι, καὶ καταφωρῷτο διψῶν, ἃ ἂν βούλοιτο δρᾷν αὐτός. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Σύμφημι· νοεῖς γὰρ ὀρθῶς. {ΚΥΡ.} Ἐπὶ προβάτῳ δὲ αὖ, καὶ μὴν καὶ αἰγὶ, τὸν αὐτὸν ὁρίζει νόμον, καὶ ἐν ἴσῳ τρόπῳ καὶ ἐπ' αὐτοῖς τὰ τῆς θυσίας ἐπράττετο, τῆς τῶν ζώων ὡς ἐν μεγέθει διαφορᾶς, τῶν καρποφορεῖν εἰωθότων, τὸ ἐν εὐσεβείᾳ τε καὶ εὐδοκιμήσει μέτρον ὑποφαινούσης ἀστείως· ὁ μὲν γὰρ, πλουσίως καὶ ὑπερφερῶς, ὡς ἔν γε τῷ μόσχῳ, περινοεῖν ἄξιον· ὁ δὲ μέσως, ὡς ἐν προβάτῳ, ὁ δὲ καὶ ὑφειμένως ἔτι· μείων γὰρ αἲξ προβάτου· καὶ τοῦτο, οἶμαι, ἐστὶ τὸ τὴν εὔκαρπον ἀναφῦναι γῆν ἑκατὸν, καὶ ἑξήκοντα, καὶ τριάκοντα, κατά γε τὴν ἐν τοῖς Εὐαγγελίοις παραβολήν. {ΠΑΛΛ.} Πείθομαι. {ΚΥΡ.} Ὅτι δὲ καὶ ἀναλόγως τοῖς ἑκάστου κατορθώμασιν ἡ τῆς ἀμοιβῆς ἀντέκτισις, καὶ ἰσοπαλεῖς τοῖς ἱδρῶσιν αἱ ἀμοιβαὶ τοῖς ἀνδραγαθεῖν ᾑρημένοις ἐκνεμηθήσονται παρὰ Θεοῦ, πληροφορήσει μὲν καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ Σωτὴρ, τὴν τῶν ταλάντων διανομὴν οὐκ ἐν ἴσῳ τρόπῳ γενέσθαι λέγων, καθιστὰς δὲ τῶν εὐδοκιμούντων, τὸν μὲν ἐπὶ δέκα πόλεων, τὸν δ' ἐπὶ πέντε. Ταλαντεύεται γὰρ ὥσπερ ὁ ἑκάστου βίος, καὶ ἰσοστατήσει που πάντως ταῖς ἡμῶν ἐπιεικείαις ἡ ἀντέκτι
pass_a_gloss: [completing §9’s last sentence] … fills (ἐμπίπλημι) the mind (φρήν) of the saints. Therefore they would become both sacred (ἱεροί) and choice/set apart (ἐξαίρετοι) for God for a smell of fragrance. Kidneys again would be for a type of the discerning activity (διακριτικὴ ἐνέργεια) inward in the mind (νοῦς); according to which one makes (ποιέομαι) to be rejected (ἀπόβλητον) what is naturally apt to wrong/harm (ἀδικέω), and choiceworthy (αἱρετόν) and worth taking (ἀξιόληπτον) what benefits (ὠφελέω). And the inspired Paul writes: ‘Testing (δοκιμάζω) all things, hold fast (κατέχω) the good (τὸ καλόν); from every form (εἶδος) of evil (πονηρόν) abstain (ἀπέχομαι).’ So since the kidney is a discerning part (μόριον) in the body (for it separates (ἀποκρίνω) very well the superfluous (τὰ περιττά), putting into (ἐνίημι) the nature (φύσις) the useful (χρηστόν) and beneficial, and distributing (διανέμω) skillfully (εὐτέχνως) to whom and how much it is fitting to be distributed), the kidneys must fittingly be transferred (μεταληπτέον) to discernment of mind (νοῦ διάκρισις). Sacred then and a dedicated offering (ἀνάθημα) to God the kidneys of the saints, that is, the discernment they would have in the mind. For approved (δόκιμοι) and exact (ἀκριβεῖς) money changers (τραπεζῖται) are those devoted (πρόσκειμαι) to God, condemning as counterfeit (κατακιβδηλεύω) always the worthless (φαῦλον), but accustomed to honor with the all-fair vote (ψῆφος πάγκαλος) what tends to profit (ὄνησις). Thus, I think, the inspired Singer (Μελῳδός), accustomed to be approved (εὐδοκιμέω), cried aloud (διακράζω) to God: ‘For You possessed/acquired (κτάομαι) my kidneys, Lord.’ The lobe of the liver shows (ὑποφαίνω) to us nothing less than an activity of soul (ψυχῆς ἐνέργεια), or movement of mind (φρενὸς κίνησις), according to which it goes (ἵεμαι) toward desires (ἐπιθυμίαι). Some having examined closely (ἐξακριβόω) such things say without hesitating (ὀκνέω) that every living thing (ζῷον) has its desires in the liver. One must dedicate (ἀναθετέον) the lobe of the liver also to God, that is, as it were the very spring (πηγή) of all our desire, according to the Singer who sings: ‘Lord, before You is all my desire.’ Someone takes pride (σεμνύνομαι) in himself and sings out (ἀναμέλπω) the voice so august (σεπτή) and admirable (ἀξιάγαστος), if he should have his longings (ὀρέξεις) toward only what seems good (δοκοῦν) to God, and be caught (καταφωράω) thirsting (διψάω) for what He Himself would wish to do/be done (δρᾶν). PALL.: I agree (σύμφημι); for you understand rightly. CYR.: For sheep (πρόβατον) again, and indeed goat (αἴξ), he defines (ὁρίζω) the same law, and in equal manner for them the things of the sacrifice were done, the difference (διαφορά) of the animals as in size (μέγεθος) elegantly (ἀστείως) suggesting the measure (μέτρον) in piety (εὐσέβεια) and approval (εὐδοκίμησις) of those accustomed to bear fruit (καρποφορέω): for the one, richly (πλουσίως) and surpassingly (ὑπερφερῶς), as in the calf, it is worth considering; the other moderately (μέσως), as in sheep; the other lower still (ὑφειμένως); for a goat is less than a sheep; and this, I think, is the fruitful (εὔκαρπος) earth sprouting up (ἀναφύω) a hundred and sixty and thirty, according to the parable (παραβολή) in the Gospels. PALL.: I am persuaded (πείθομαι). CYR.: That the repayment (ἀντέκτισις) of recompense (ἀμοιβή) is in proportion (ἀναλόγως) to the right deeds (κατορθώματα) of each, and rewards equal-matched (ἰσοπαλεῖς) to the sweats will be allotted (ἐκνέμω) from God to those who choose to act bravely (ἀνδραγαθέω), the Savior Himself will fully assure (πληροφορέω), saying that the distribution (διανομή) of the talents (τάλαντα) did not happen in equal manner, and establishing (καθίστημι) of those who did well one over ten cities, another over five. For each one’s life is weighed (ταλαντεύομαι) as it were, and the repayment (ἀντέκτισις, word split: ἀντέκτι-|σις §11) will surely balance equally (ἰσοστατέω) with our goodnesses/fair dealings (ἐπιείκειαι).
pass_b_english: Cyril: So they would become holy, and set apart for God as a fragrant aroma. The kidneys, again, would be a type of the activity of discernment within the mind, by which one rejects what by nature does harm, and counts what is beneficial as worth choosing and taking. And the inspired Paul writes: ‘Test all things; hold fast what is good; keep away from every form of evil’ (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22). So since the kidney is a part of the body that discerns (for it separates out what is surplus very well, lets what is wholesome and useful into the body, and distributes it with art to the parts that should receive it, and in the right amount), we must with good reason take the kidneys to mean the discernment of the mind. Holy, then, and an offering dedicated to God are the kidneys of the saints, that is, the discernment they have in the mind. For those who cleave to God are approved and exact money changers: they always reject what is worthless as counterfeit, but they are accustomed to honor with their excellent verdict whatever leads to benefit. It was in this way, I think, that the inspired Psalmist, who was used to winning approval, cried out to God: ‘For you have taken possession of my kidneys, O Lord’ (Psalm 139:13).

The lobe of the liver, for its part, points us to nothing other than an activity of the soul, that is, a movement of the mind, by which it reaches out toward desires. Some who have studied such matters closely say without hesitation that every living creature has its desires in the liver. So the lobe of the liver too must be dedicated to God, that is, so to speak, the very source of all our desire, as the Psalmist sings: ‘Lord, all my desire is before you’ (Psalm 38:9). And a person takes pride in himself and sings out so solemn and admirable a word if his longings are set on nothing but what pleases God, and he is found thirsting for whatever he himself may wish to do.
Palladius: I agree; you understand it rightly.

Cyril: For the sheep, in turn, and for the goat as well, the Lawgiver lays down the same law, and the sacrifice was carried out in the same way for these too (Leviticus 3:6–16). The difference in size among the animals neatly points to the measure of piety and approval among those who are used to bearing fruit. For one person, we should think, bears fruit richly and above the rest, as in the calf; another moderately, as in the sheep; and another more modestly still, for a goat is smaller than a sheep. And this, I think, is the fruitful earth yielding a hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold, as in the parable in the Gospels (Matthew 13:8).

Cyril: That the repayment of reward will be in proportion to each one’s good deeds, and that God will allot to those who have chosen to act nobly rewards matched to their labors, the Savior himself will assure us. He says that the talents were not handed out in equal shares (Matthew 25:15), and of those who did well he sets one over ten cities and another over five (Luke 19:17–19). For each one’s life is weighed, as it were, in the balance, and the repayment will surely be equal in weight to our goodness.

apparatus.note: PG OCR; a column may cut mid-sentence or mid-word.

PG 68.1028. Boundary in: the opening words τῶν ἁγίων ἐμπίπλησι φρένα complete the last sentence of section 9 and are rendered there; this section’s English starts with Τοιγάρτοι. Boundary out: the section ends inside the word ἀντέκτι|σις (‘repayment’), finished by the syllable σις that opens section 11; the whole word is rendered here, so section 11 starts with οὐδὲν δὲ ἧττον (‘and no less…’). The subject of ‘they would become holy’ is the saints whose minds are filled with good (end of section 9); ἐξαίρετοι (‘choice, set apart’) may also play on ἐξαιρέω, the removing of the fat. LXX renumbering: Psalm 138:13 LXX = Psalm 139:13 (Hebrew-based Bibles read ‘you formed my inward parts’; the LXX ἐκτήσω ‘took possession of’ and νεφροί ‘kidneys’ are kept because Cyril’s argument rests on them); Psalm 37:10 LXX = Psalm 38:9. ‘Approved money changers’ (δόκιμοι τραπεζῖται) echoes the well-known unwritten saying ‘Be approved money changers’, found in many early writers but not in the canonical Gospels; no citation given. The view that the desires lodge in the liver is Platonic (Timaeus 70d–72b) and widespread in ancient medicine; Cyril names no source. Ὧδε … εὐδοκιμεῖν εἰωθότα is rendered ‘It was in this way … that the inspired Psalmist, who was used to winning approval, cried out’; it could also mean that his approval came from this kind of discernment. Ἃ ἂν βούλοιτο δρᾶν αὐτός is ambiguous: αὐτός may be God (‘whatever he himself may wish to do’, adopted, since the clause before speaks of what pleases God) or the person (‘what he himself would want to do’). Ἐπὶ προβάτῳ … καὶ αἰγί refers to Leviticus 3:6–11 (sheep) and 3:12–16 (goat); the subject of ὁρίζει is the Lawgiver, made explicit in English. The order hundred, sixty, thirty matches Matthew 13:8 (and 13:23), not Mark 4:8. Cyril joins two parables: the unequal talents (Matthew 25:15) and the rule over ten and five cities, which belongs to the parable of the pounds (Luke 19:17–19). Ταλαντεύεται (‘is weighed’) plays on τάλαντα (‘talents’); the pun is lost in English. Ἐπιείκειαι rendered ‘goodness’, as in section 4.
